title: Of books
paragraphs: I have no doubt that I often happen to speak of things that are handled much better, and more truthfully, by those who are masters of the trade. What you have here is purely an essay of my natural parts, not of those acquired by study; and whoever catches me tripping in ignorance will get no advantage over me, for I would be very unwilling to be answerable to anyone else for my writings, since I am not answerable to myself, nor satisfied with them. Whoever goes hunting after knowledge, let him fish for it where it is to be found; there is nothing I so little profess. These are fancies of my own, by which I do not pretend to discover things but to lay myself open; they may, one day, be known to me, or may have been once, depending on whether fortune brought me to the place where they were explained — but I have utterly forgotten it. If I am a man of some reading, I am a man of no retention. So I can promise no certainty beyond making known to what point the knowledge I now have has risen. Therefore let no one lay weight on the matter I write, but on my method of writing it. Let them observe, in what I borrow, whether I have known how to choose what suits to lift or help the invention, which is always my own. For I make others say for me, not before but after me, what — for want of either language or sense — I cannot myself express so well. I do not count my borrowings; I weigh them. If I had wanted to raise their value by number I would have made them twice as many. They are nearly all from such famous and ancient authors that they seem, I think, to identify themselves without my having to do the work. In reasons, comparisons, and arguments, if I transplant any into my own soil and mingle them with my own, I deliberately hide the author, to keep in check the recklessness of those snap critics who fall on every kind of writing, particularly the recent ones, by men still living, and in the common tongue, which puts everyone in a position to criticise and seems to convict the conception and design of being vulgar too. I want them to give Plutarch a flick on the nose, and to rail at Seneca when they think they are railing at me. I have to shelter my own weakness under these great reputations. I will love anyone who can strip my plumage from me — that is, by clearness of understanding and judgment, and purely by distinguishing the force and beauty of the words. For I, who for lack of memory am at every turn unable to pick them out by their national livery, am nevertheless wise enough to know, by the measure of my own abilities, that my soil is incapable of producing any of those rich flowers I find growing there, and that all the fruits of my own growth are not worth one of them. For this much, indeed, I hold myself responsible: if I get in my own way; if there is any vanity or defect in my writings that I do not myself perceive nor can recognise when pointed out by another. Many faults escape our eye, but the weakness of judgment consists in being unable to see them once another lays them open. Knowledge and truth can be in us without judgment, and judgment without them; but the confession of ignorance is one of the finest and surest signs of judgment that I know. I have no other officer to put my writings in rank and file, only chance. As things come into my head, I heap them one on top of another; sometimes they advance in whole bodies, sometimes in single file. I would have everyone see my natural and ordinary pace, irregular as it is; I let myself jog on at my own rate. Nor are these subjects in which one is forbidden to be ignorant, or to speak of casually and at random. I could wish for a more complete knowledge of things, but I will not pay for it at the price it costs. My plan is to pass over the remainder of my life easily, not laboriously; there is nothing I will rack my brains about, not even knowledge, however valuable.
In reading books, I seek only to please myself by an honest diversion; or, if I study, it is for no other science than what treats of knowing myself and instructs me how to die and how to live well.
"Has meus ad metas sudet oportet equus."
["My horse must sweat to keep my pace." — Propertius, iv.]

I do not bite my nails over the difficulties I meet with in my reading; after a charge or two, I give them up. If I kept at them, I would lose both myself and time, for I have an impatient understanding that has to be satisfied at first attempt: what I do not grasp at once is only made more obscure by persistence. I do nothing without good cheer; continuation and a too obstinate effort darken, stupefy, and tire my judgment. My sight is confounded and dispersed by staring; I have to withdraw it and refer my discovery to fresh attempts — just as, to judge of the lustre of scarlet rightly, we are taught to pass the eye lightly over it and then to run it across again in several sudden and repeated glances. If one book does not please me, I take another; and I never touch any of them except when I am tired of doing nothing. I do not much care for new ones, because the old ones seem fuller and stronger; nor do I converse much with Greek authors, because my judgment cannot do its work on imperfect comprehension of the material.

Among books that are simply pleasant, of the moderns, Boccaccio's Decameron, Rabelais, and the Basia of Johannes Secundus (if those can be classed under that heading) are worth reading for amusement. As for the Amadis and that kind of stuff, they did not have enough credit to arrest even my childhood. And I will say further, whether boldly or rashly, that this old, heavy soul of mine is no longer tickled by Ariosto, no, not even by the worthy Ovid; his facility and inventions, which once ravished me, are now no longer to my taste, and I can hardly have the patience to read him. I speak my opinion freely about everything, even about things that perhaps exceed my capacity and that I do not consider in any way under my jurisdiction. Accordingly, the judgment I deliver is meant to show the measure of my own sight, not of the things I am so bold as to criticise. When I find myself put off by Plato's Axiochus, as by a work — with all due respect to such an author — without force, my judgment does not believe itself: it is not so arrogant as to set itself against the authority of so many other famous judgments of antiquity, which it considers its tutors and masters, and with whom it is rather content to err. In such a case, it condemns itself either to stop at the outer bark, being unable to penetrate to the heart, or to consider the work by some false light. It is content with only sparing itself trouble and confusion; as to its own weakness, it frankly acknowledges and confesses it. It thinks it gives a just interpretation to the appearances presented to it by its own conceptions, but they are weak and imperfect. Most of Aesop's fables have several senses and meanings, of which the mythologists chose some one that fits the fable; but for the most part, this is only the first face that presents itself, and a superficial one; there still remain others, more vivid, essential, and profound, into which they have not been able to penetrate. And so it is with me.

But to keep to the business of this essay: I have always thought that, in poetry, Virgil, Lucretius, Catullus, and Horace by many degrees outshine the rest; and especially Virgil in his Georgics, which I take to be the most accomplished piece in poetry — by comparison with which one can easily see that there are some places in his Aeneid to which the author would have given a little more of the file, had he had leisure; and the fifth book of his Aeneid seems to me the most perfect. I also love Lucan, and willingly read him, not so much for his style as for his own worth, and for the truth and solidity of his opinions and judgments. As for good Terence — the refined elegance and grace of the Latin tongue — I find him admirable in his vivid depiction of our manners and the movements of the soul; our own actions throw me back upon him at every turn, and I cannot read him so often that I do not still find some new grace and beauty. Those who lived near Virgil's time complained that some compared Lucretius with him. I am of the opinion that the comparison is, in truth, very unequal — though I have a hard time convincing myself of it when I come across some excellent passage in Lucretius. But if they were so angry at that comparison, what would they say to the brutish, barbarous stupidity of those who, nowadays, compare him with Ariosto? Would not Ariosto himself say:
"O seclum insipiens et inficetum!"
["O stupid and tasteless age." — Catullus, xliii. 8.]

I think the ancients had more reason to be angry at those who compared Plautus with Terence, though that comparison was much closer than the one between Lucretius and Virgil. It counts for the estimation and preference of Terence that the father of Roman eloquence has him so often, and alone of his class, on his lips — and the opinion the best judge of Roman poets passed on his companion. I have often noticed that those of our day who take it upon themselves to write comedies (in imitation of the Italians, who are happy enough in that line) take three or four plots from Plautus or Terence to make one of their own, and crowd five or six of Boccaccio's novellas into a single comedy. What makes them load themselves with so much material is the lack of confidence they have in their own ability to support themselves on their own strength. They have to find something to lean on; and not having stuff of their own to entertain us with, they bring in the story to make up for the want of language. With my author, it is quite the other way: the elegance and perfection of his speech makes us lose our appetite for his plot; his refined grace and elegance of style occupy us everywhere; he is so pleasant throughout —
"Liquidus, puroque simillimus amni,"
["Clear and most like a pure river." — Horace, Ep., ii. 2, 120.]

and so possesses the soul with his graces that we forget those of his story. This same consideration carries me further: I notice that the best of the ancient poets avoided affectation and the hunt after, not only fantastic Spanish and Petrarchan flights, but even those softer and gentler touches that are the ornament of all subsequent poetry. And yet there is no sound judgment that will condemn this in the ancients, and that does not incomparably more admire the even polish and that perpetual sweetness and flourishing beauty of Catullus's epigrams, than all the stings with which Martial arms the tails of his. The reason is the one I gave before, and as Martial himself says of himself:
"Minus illi ingenio laborandum fuit, in cujus locum materia successerat:"
["His wit had less work to do, because the subject itself supplied what was needed." — Martial, praef. ad lib. viii.]

The first sort, without being moved, without getting angry, make themselves sufficiently felt; they have laughter enough throughout, without having to tickle themselves; the others need outside assistance. The less wit they have, the more body they need; they get on horseback because they cannot stand on their own legs. Just as in our balls, those mean fellows who teach dancing, unable to represent the bearing and dignity of our nobility, are reduced to throwing themselves forward with dangerous leaps and other strange motions and tumblers' tricks; and the ladies are less troubled in dances where there are various coupees, changes, and quick body-movements, than in some other, more sedate kind, where they only have to move at a natural pace and represent their ordinary grace and presence. So I have seen good comic actors who, in their everyday clothes and with the same face they always wear, give us all the pleasure of their art, while their apprentices, not yet arrived at such a pitch, are obliged to plaster their faces, put on absurd disguises, and make a hundred grotesque grimaces to give us something to laugh at. This idea of mine is nowhere more demonstrable than in comparing the Aeneid with Orlando Furioso: the first, by dint of wing, flies in a brave and lofty place and always keeps to his point; the latter, fluttering and hopping from tale to tale, as from branch to branch, daring to trust his wings only in very short flights, perching at every turn lest his breath and strength fail him.
"Excursusque breves tentat."
["And he attempts short excursions." — Virgil, Georgics, iv. 194.]
These, then, as to this sort of subject, are the authors who please me best.

As to the rest of my reading, which mixes a little more profit with the pleasure, and through which I learn how to order my opinions and conduct, the books that serve me to this purpose are Plutarch (since he was translated into French) and Seneca. Both have this notable convenience suited to my temperament, that the knowledge I seek there is set out in loose pieces, not requiring long stretches of reading, of which I am incapable. Such are the minor works of the first and the Epistles of the second, which are the best and most profitable of all their writings. It is no great undertaking to pick one of them up, and I leave off at pleasure, for there is no sequence or dependence between the pieces. These authors for the most part agree in useful and true opinions; and there is this parallel between them — that fortune brought them into the world around the same century, that they were both tutors to two Roman emperors, both fetched from foreign countries, both rich, both great men. Their instruction is the cream of philosophy, delivered in a plain and pertinent way. Plutarch is more uniform and steady; Seneca more various and shifting: the latter toiled and bent his whole strength to fortify virtue against weakness, fear, and vicious appetites; the former seems more to slight their power, and disdains to alter his pace or stand on his guard. Plutarch's opinions are Platonic, gentle, accommodated to civil society; the other's are Stoic and Epicurean, further from common use, but in my opinion more personally serviceable and more firm. Seneca seems to lean a little toward the tyranny of the emperors of his time — but only seems; for I take it as certain that he speaks against his own judgment when he condemns the act of the generous murderers of Caesar. Plutarch is frank throughout; Seneca abounds in lively touches and sallies; Plutarch in things that warm and move you more; this one contents and pays you better — he guides us, the other pushes us on.

As to Cicero, his works most useful to my purpose are those that treat of manners and the rules of our life. But to confess the truth boldly (since one has crossed the barriers of impudence, there is no holding back), his way of writing strikes me as careless and uninviting; his prefaces, definitions, divisions, and etymologies take up most of his work, and whatever there is of life and marrow is smothered and lost in the long preparation. When I have spent an hour reading him — which is a great deal for me — and try to recollect what juice and substance I have extracted, for the most part I find nothing but wind. He has not yet come to the arguments that serve his purpose, nor to the reasons that properly help to form the knot I am after. For me, who only want to become wiser, not more learned or eloquent, these logical and Aristotelian arrangements of parts are of no use. I would have a man start with the main proposition. I know well enough what death and pleasure are; let no one go to the trouble of dissecting them for me. I look for good, solid reasons, at the first stroke, to teach me how to stand their shock — for which neither grammatical subtleties nor the quaint texture of words and arguments are of any use at all. I am for discourses that drive the first charge into the heart of the redoubt; his languish about the subject. They are well enough for the schools, the bar, and the pulpit, where we have leisure to nod and may wake up a quarter of an hour later in time to find the thread of the discourse again. One must speak this way to judges, whom one means to win over by right or wrong, to children and the common people, to whom one must say everything and see what comes of it. I would not have an author make it his business to render me attentive, or cry "Oyez!" fifty times, as the heralds do. The Romans in their religious exercises began with Hoc age, as we in ours do with Sursum corda; these are so many words wasted on me — I come fully prepared from my chamber. I need no allurement, no invitation, no sauce; I eat the meat raw, so that, instead of whetting my appetite, these preparations tire and dull it. Will the licence of the times excuse my sacrilegious boldness if I find even Plato's dialogues themselves dull and heavy, smothering the matter too much, and lament so much time lost by a man who had so many better things to say, in so many long and needless preliminary exchanges? My ignorance excuses me better here, in that I do not know Greek well enough to discern the beauty of his language. I generally choose books that use sciences, not those that only lead to them. The two first, and Pliny, and their like, have none of this Hoc age; they want to deal with men already instructed; or if they do offer it, it is a substantial Hoc age, with a body of its own. I also delight in reading the Letters to Atticus, not only because they contain a great deal of the history and affairs of his time, but much more because in them I uncover much of his own private temper; for I have a singular curiosity, as I have said elsewhere, to pry into the souls and the natural, true opinions of the authors with whom I converse. One may judge their parts, but not their manners or themselves, by the writings they display on the theatre of the world. I have a thousand times lamented the loss of the treatise Brutus wrote on Virtue, for it is well to learn the theory from those who best know the practice.

But since the matter preached and the preacher are different things, I would as gladly see Brutus in Plutarch as in a book of his own. I would rather be certainly informed of the conversation he had in his tent with some particular friends of his the night before a battle, than of the harangue he made to his army the next day; and of what he did in his study and chamber, than of what he did in the public square and in the senate. As to Cicero, I am of the common opinion that, learning aside, he had no great natural excellence. He was a good citizen, of an affable nature, as all fat, heavy men such as he was usually are; but given to ease, and had in truth a mighty share of vanity and ambition. Nor do I know how to excuse him for thinking his poetry fit to be published; it is no great fault to make bad verses, but it is a fault not to be able to judge how unworthy his verses were of the glory of his name. As for his eloquence, that is wholly beyond comparison, and I believe it will never be equalled. The younger Cicero, who resembled his father in nothing but the name, was once commanding in Asia, and had several strangers at his table, with Cestius seated at the lower end, as people often intrude at the open tables of the great. Cicero asked one of his people who that man was, who promptly told him the name; but he, as one whose thoughts were taken up with something else and who had forgotten the answer given him, asked the same question three or four times over. The fellow, to deliver himself from so many answers and to make him remember the man by some particular detail, said, "It is that Cestius, of whom you were told that he makes no great account of your father's eloquence in comparison with his own." At which Cicero, suddenly stung, ordered poor Cestius to be seized at once, and had him very well whipped in his own presence — a very discourteous host! Yet even among those who, all things considered, have reputed his eloquence incomparable, there have been some who have not hesitated to note some faults in it: as that great Brutus, his friend, for example, who said it was a broken and feeble eloquence, fractam et elumbem. The orators nearest to the age in which he lived also reproached him for the care he took with a certain long cadence in his periods, and particularly noticed his repeated use of the words esse videatur. For my part, I prefer a shorter style, that comes off more roundly. He does sometimes shuffle his parts more briskly together, but very seldom. I have myself noted this one passage:
"Ego vero me minus diu senem mallem, quam esse senem, antequam essem."
["I would rather be old for a short time than be old before I was old." — Cicero, De Senect., c. 10.]
The historians are my right ball, for they are pleasant and easy, and in them man in general — the knowledge of whom I hunt after — appears more vividly and whole than anywhere else:
[The easiest of my amusements — the right ball at tennis being the one that, coming to the player from the right hand, is much easier to play. — Coste.]

the variety and truth of his inner qualities, both in bulk and piecemeal; the diversity of means by which he is held together and knit; and the accidents that threaten him. Now those who write lives, because they insist more on counsels than on events, more on what comes out from within than on what happens without, are the most suitable for my reading; and so, above all others, Plutarch is the man for me. I am very sorry we do not have a dozen Laertiuses, or that he was not more extended; for I am equally curious to know the lives and fortunes of these great instructors of the world as to know the varieties of their doctrines and opinions. In this kind of study of histories, one must tumble over, without distinction, all sorts of authors — old and new, French or foreign — to learn the matters they variously treat. But Caesar, in my opinion, particularly deserves to be studied, not only for the knowledge of the history but for himself, so great is his excellence and perfection over all the rest, though Sallust is one of the number. In earnest, I read this author with more reverence and respect than is usually allowed to human writings: now considering him in his person, by his actions and his miraculous greatness; now in the purity and inimitable polish of his language, in which he excels not only all other historians, as Cicero confesses, but, perhaps, Cicero himself. He speaks of his enemies with so much sincerity in his judgment that — apart from the false colours with which he tries to gloss over his evil cause, and the filth of his pestilent ambition — I think there is no fault to be objected to him, save this: that he speaks too sparingly of himself, seeing that so many great things could not have been accomplished under his conduct without his own personal acts having had a greater share than he attributes to them.

I love historians, whether of the simple sort or of the higher order. The simple, who have nothing of their own to mix in and only make it their business to collect everything that comes to their knowledge and to record all things faithfully, without choice or discrimination, leave us the whole judgment of discerning the truth. Such, for example, is honest Froissart, who has proceeded in his work with such frank plainness that, having committed an error, he is not ashamed to confess and correct it where the finger has been laid; he even reports for us the variety of rumours that were going around and the different accounts given to him. This is the naked and unformed matter of history, of which everyone may make his profit according to his understanding. The more excellent sort of historians have judgment to pick out what is most worthy of being known and, of two reports, to examine which is most likely true; from the condition of princes and their tempers they deduce their counsels, and assign them words appropriate to the occasion. Such have title to claim the authority of regulating our belief by what they themselves believe; but certainly this privilege belongs to very few. As for the middle sort, of which most are, they spoil everything; they want to chew our meat for us; they take it upon themselves to judge of, and consequently to incline, the history to their own fancy. For if the judgment leans one way, one cannot avoid wresting and twisting the narrative to that bias. They undertake to select things worthy of being known, and yet often hide from us such a word, such a private action, as would much better instruct us; they omit, as incredible, things they do not understand, and some, perhaps, because they cannot put them into good French or Latin. Let them display their eloquence and intelligence, and judge according to their own fancy; but let them also leave us something to judge of after them, and neither alter nor disguise, by their abridgments and choices, anything of the substance of the matter, but deliver it to us pure and entire in all its dimensions.

For the most part, and especially in these recent ages, people are picked out for this work from among the common sort on the sole consideration of well-speaking, as if we were to learn grammar from them; and the men so chosen have fair reason — being hired for nothing else, and pretending to nothing but babble — not to be very concerned with anything but that, so that, with a fine jingle of words, they prepare for us a pretty piece of reports they pick up in the streets. The only good histories are those written by men who held command in the affairs they write about, or who took part in conducting them, or at least had the conduct of others of the same kind. Such are almost all the Greek and Roman histories: for, several eyewitnesses having written on the same subject, in a time when grandeur and learning commonly met in the same person, if any error has crept in it must of necessity be a very slight one, and on a very doubtful incident. What can one expect from a physician writing of war, or from a mere scholar treating of the designs of princes? If we wanted to note how scrupulous the Romans were in this matter, only one example would be needed: Asinius Pollio found in the histories of Caesar himself something misreported — a mistake caused either by Caesar's inability to have his eye in every part of his army at once, having credited certain individuals who had given him an inaccurate account, or by his not having had a sufficiently exact account from his lieutenants of what they had done in his absence. From this we may see how delicate the search for truth is, when one cannot trust the report of a battle from the knowledge of the man who commanded there, nor from the soldiers who were engaged in it, unless, after the method of a judicial enquiry, the witnesses are confronted and objections weighed on each least detail of every incident. In good earnest, the knowledge we have of our own affairs is much more obscure; but this has been sufficiently dealt with by Bodin, and according to my own view. To support a little the weakness of my memory (which is so extreme that more than once I have happened to pick up books again as new and unseen, that I had carefully read a few years before and scribbled over with my notes), I have lately adopted the custom of noting at the end of every book (that is, of those I never intend to read again) the time when I finished it and the judgment I had formed of it, so that this might at least represent to me the character and general idea I had conceived of the author in reading it; and I will copy out some of those notes here.

I wrote this, some ten years ago, in my Guicciardini (whatever language my books speak to me in, I always speak to them in my own): "He is a diligent historian, from whom, in my opinion, one may learn the truth of the affairs of his time as exactly as from any other; in most of which he was himself a personal actor, and in honourable command. There is no sign that he disguised anything out of hatred, favour, or vanity; of which the free verdicts he passes on the great ones, especially those by whom he was promoted and employed in offices of great trust and honour, like Pope Clement VII, give ample testimony. As for the part he thinks himself best at — namely, his digressions and discourses — he has some very good ones, enriched with fine touches; but he is too fond of them. For, leaving nothing unsaid, with a subject so full, ample, almost infinite, he degenerates into pedantry and smacks a little of scholastic prattle. I have also noticed this in him: that of so many souls and so many effects, so many motives and so many counsels as he judges, he never attributes any one to virtue, religion, or conscience — as if all these were utterly extinct in the world. Of all the actions, however brave they appear in outward show, he always traces the cause and motive to some vicious occasion or some prospect of profit. It is impossible to think that, among such an infinite number of actions as he mentions, there should not be some produced by way of honest reason. No corruption could so universally have infected men that some would not escape the contagion; which makes me suspect that his own taste was vicious, from which it may have happened that he judged other men by himself."

In my Philippe de Commines is written: "You will find the language here sweet and pleasant, with a natural simplicity; the narration pure, with the good faith of the author conspicuous throughout — free from vanity when he speaks of himself, and from partiality or envy when he speaks of others; his discourses and exhortations accompanied rather by zeal and truth than by any exquisite ability; and, throughout, authority and gravity that bespeak a man of good extraction, brought up in great affairs."

On the Memoirs of Monsieur du Bellay I have this: "It is always pleasant to read things written by those who have experienced how they should be conducted; but it cannot be denied that there is a manifest falling-off in these two lords from the freedom and liberty of writing that shine in the earlier historians — such as the Sieur de Joinville, the familiar companion of St Louis; Eginhard, chancellor to Charlemagne; and, more recently, Philippe de Commines. What we have here is rather an apology for King Francis, against the Emperor Charles V, than history. I will not believe that they falsified anything as to matter of fact; but they make a common practice of twisting the judgment of events, often against reason, to our advantage, and of leaving out whatever is ticklish to handle in their master's life — witness the affairs of Messieurs de Montmorency and de Biron, which are omitted here; even the very name of Madame d'Étampes is not to be found. Secret actions a historian may keep quiet; but to pass over in silence what all the world knows, and things that have drawn after them public and momentous consequences, is an inexcusable defect. In short, whoever wants a thorough knowledge of King Francis and the events of his reign, let him seek it elsewhere, if my advice prevails. The only profit one can reap from these Memoirs is in the particular accounts of the battles and other exploits of war in which these gentlemen were personally engaged; in some words and private actions of the princes of their time; and in the treaties and negotiations carried out by the Seigneur de Langey, where there are things everywhere worth knowing, and discourses above the common strain."
